newsitem.title: UK: UK's Rifkind moves to damp down new Euro row.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind moves to damp down new Euro row.

text.p: A senior British government minister on Friday attempted to damp down a row in the ruling Conservative Party over a cabinet colleague's call for a more critical stance towards Europe.
Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell's demand that Britain negotiate a new relationship with its European partners did not run counter to government policy.
"He does not see the European Union purely as a free trade area," Rifkind said on BBC radio. "It has to be more than a free trade area but must never become a European state."
Rifkind added; "His position, so far as I am aware, is exactly the same as the cabinet as a whole."
Friday's newspapers accused Dorrell of jockeying for position ahead of a post-election Conservative leadership battle by adopting a tougher line on Europe.

The new row over Europe, always a divisive topic for the Conservatives, threatened to overshadow a pledge by Prime Minister John Major make the rights of families a central theme in the imminent general election campagn.
Dorrell, once on the pro-European wing of the ruling party, called on Thursday for Britain to review its links with its European Union partners.

The move delighted the party's right wing. But it suggested that the arrival of election year -- Major must call a poll by May 22 -- has failed to moderate Conservative feuding over Europe which for months has marred their electoral prospects.

"We need to negotiate with our partners a relationship into the next century which reflects the reality of the next century -- that is to say the need to win in a much more flexible and competitive market place," Dorrell said.
The Times said the statement was "a crude attempt by Mr Dorrell to position himself for a Tory leadership election".

And the Daily Express said: "Mr Dorrell may well be preparing for the leadership race which will follow a Tory election defeat...he is also conceding that he sees which way the wind is blowing in the Tory Party."
Opposition Labour Party deputy leader John Prescott agreed. "He has jumped ship and now wants to get in the race." he said.
Major is expected to step down as leader if the Conservatives, some 20 points behind Labour in the polls, are forced out of power for the first time in almost 18 years.

A host of senior Conservatives could join battle to replace him, ranging from pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke to John Redwood, the right-winger who resigned from the cabinet in 1995 to challenge Major for the leadership.
In an article in the Daily Telegraph, Major insisted his party was united on fundamental principles such as the need to preserve family values and traditional institutions.
"Whatever our sincerely-held differences may be on particular issues, those of us who are drawn to the Conservative cause know the power of the bonds that bind us together," he said.
